keep: The idea is named up front: two moves make one move, its matrix is the product, and AB reads right to left, B first.
The cause is shown, not just the effect: each move keeps the grid a grid with the origin fixed, so the pair is one linear transformation whose columns are where i and j end up.

One worked example computed from the rule, the brief's own: a quarter turn then the shear gives [1 −1; 1 0], and the shear then the turn gives [0 −1; 1 1], each found by following i and j and checked by row times column in practice.

The order slip is shown failing (screen 4's trap is AB again), the left-to-right reading has its own puzzle (screen 6), and the entry-by-entry slip is a wrong pick on screen 8 beside the adding screen.
No false absolute: 'usually' on the order, with the identity and two turns named as pairs that agree either way. A 2 by 2 matrix cannot slide anything, which holds for every one.

Twelve screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and DO, ending on two mixed puzzles. The analogy is from the bench and says where it breaks. Two footnotes, each on a rule he might look up, and no source named in the text.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'Column 1 of AB is where A sends column 1 of B' needs its reason. B sends i to B's column 1, so A then moves that point. Say it in a sentence.

The arithmetic paragraph runs three ideas together (row times column, sizes, adding) and its 'So each row of A must be as long…' does not follow from the example. Split it: row times column with its reason, then the size rule because a row meets a column pair by pair, then adding in its own short paragraph.

Hints: the DO screens with a named slip need their own one-line hint in the brief. Screen 4 (order assumed not to matter), screen 6 (reading left to right), screen 8 (matching entries) and screen 11 (row read as a landing spot).
Read-through: screens 1, 5 and 7 have Play, Swap, card choices and Next. Each needs a still and a read sentence that makes sense with no controls.
numbers: several shown numbers are missing, i's end (1, 1), the multiplier 2, D's size, and the wrong picks [4 5; 2 3], (1, 1) and (−1, −1). List them.
The analogy's quarter turn has no direction. Say clockwise, so the two orders are a fair test.
